A public health campaign weaponized as a moral panic. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed faces attacks over his 2018 call to reform Michigan's outdated HIV disclosure laws.
Evidence: Public Health, Political Attack, Stigma Reduction
#Aletheia #USPol

Opponents and media outlets frame El-Sayed's 2018 call to repeal HIV criminalization as an attempt to legalize reckless transmission and endanger the public.
Stated Judgement: (-0.75, -0.60) — Lesser Evil

El-Sayed advocated for modernizing the law to align with modern science, which actually passed with broad bipartisan support in 2018 to encourage testing and destigmatize the disease.
Resulting Judgement: (+0.86, +0.94) — Greater Good

Verdict: PASS — Awakening into Grace.
The candidate's position was rooted in established epidemiological science, seeking to replace punitive stigma with effective public health solutions.
Integrity: Trustworthy (Hypocrisy: 1.1, Uncertainty z: 1)

Sub-Audits Breakdown:
- Abdul El-Sayed: PASS (0.86, 0.94) — Supported science-based reforms that became bipartisan law.
- NY Post Framing: FAIL (-0.65, -0.72) — Sensationalized past comments to imply reckless endangerment.

During his 2018 gubernatorial run, epidemiologist Abdul El-Sayed called to repeal a 1988 felony HIV law. The law was subsequently reformed by a Republican-led legislature to protect medically suppressed individuals and focus on intent.

The Bright Side:
The attack backfires by highlighting a highly successful, bipartisan public health reform that modernized Michigan's laws to reflect 21st-century medical reality.

The Plane Error: Confusing HOW we treat a disease with WHO we are punishing. The attack switches a complex epidemiological strategy (reducing stigma to increase testing) for a simplistic narrative of coddling criminals.

Social Physics Analysis:
The critics execute a Smart Selfish Maneuver, manufacturing a public safety crisis out of a successful bipartisan reform. El-Sayed's approach is Smart Altruistic, using transparency and empathy to align legal policy with medical science.

The Trajectory: The Path of Awakening into Grace.
When you map the gap between stated intentions and ground-level results, it plots a direct trajectory toward Greater Good. Science-based policy ultimately reduces transmission rates and saves lives.

The Unavoidable Truth: Criminalizing medical conditions drives transmission underground by discouraging testing.
The Unavoidable Lie: Reforming outdated laws is equivalent to encouraging the spread of disease.

Alethekanon:
Epidemiology operates on systemic feedback loops, not moralizing retribution. Punitive laws create a high-strain environment that actively defeats the goal of disease suppression.

Awwthekanon:
It is so important to treat people who are sick with love and understanding instead of fear and judgment. Reforming these laws helps people feel safe enough to seek help, get tested, and receive the care they deserve.

Brothekanon:
Using a 2018 public health debate as a political gotcha is weak. The GOP legislature literally agreed with the reform and passed it. Let's focus on actual current issues instead of rehashing old bipartisan wins.

Spirithekanon:
"Do not judge by appearances, but judge with right judgment." John 7:24 PASS
Weaponizing public health reforms as moral failures ignores the compassionate necessity of destigmatizing treatment.

Stated Claim / Post Context:
Abdul El-Sayed called for repealing law that made sex without disclosing HIV status a felony

As he unsuccessfully ran for Michigan governor in 2018, El-Sayed repeatedly took aim at the law.

Actual Article Body:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.

See more of our coverage in your search results.

Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed once called for repealing a Michigan law that made it a felony for people who knew they had HIV to have sex without first informing their partner — a position he is standing by eight years later as he campaigns in one of the nation’s most competitive Senate races.

As he unsuccessfully ran for Michigan governor in 2018, El-Sayed repeatedly took aim at the law.

The law carried a prison sentence of up to four years for people who knew they were HIV-positive and engaged in sexual penetration without first informing their partner of their HIV status.

“You should not be criminalized for a disease. That is absolutely wrong. It’s hateful. It’s discriminatory, and we can, as a state, do better. You can count on me for that,” El-Sayed said as he ran for governor.

Fast-forward eight years and El-Sayed, an epidemiologist and a former health director for Detroit-anchored Wayne County, is battling former Republican Rep. Mike Rogers in the midterm race to succeed retiring Democratic Sen. Gary Peters.

The showdown in Michigan is a must hold for the Democrats as they try to win back control of the Senate from the GOP.

As he ran for the 2018 Democratic gubernatorial nomination — a contest he lost to now-two-term Gov. Gretchen Whitmer — El-Sayed’s campaign website stated, “Repeal HIV/AIDS criminalization laws and the exclusion of transgender Michiganders from state Medicaid.”

When asked in 2018 if he supported the decriminalization of HIV through legislation that would create two levels of misdemeanors, El-Sayed said at the time, “One of the big things that we have to recognize about HIV is that no disease can be illegal.

“The continuing forward of these laws on the books stigmatize people with the disease.”

Whitmer also supported changing the law, which dated to 1988, saying as she ran for governor, “It’s wrong to criminalize sickness, which is what this law has effectively done. It absolutely should be revisited.”

The law was reformed in early 2019, after passing a GOP-controlled legislature with broad bipartisan support.

The revised statute limited the felony provisions to vaginal and anal intercourse involving an intent to transmit HIV or cases in which HIV was actually transmitted, reduced certain non-transmission offenses to misdemeanors and protected medically suppressed people from prosecution under the law’s reckless-disregard provision.

“Abdul supports the bipartisan reform bill that passed in 2019 through a Republican legislature that eliminated the discriminatory laws on the books,” campaign spokesperson Roxie Richner told Fox News Digital.

“As a public health professional, Abdul has fought to support programs that stem the spread of diseases, including HIV.”

Richner added that “the Trump administration has completely exacerbated this crisis by defunding the organizations and programs that do frontline care to prevent transmission and exposure in the first place.

“In the US Senate, Abdul will fight back against Donald Trump and RFK Jr’s attempts to dismantle our public health infrastructure and ensure all Americans have access to the care they need.”

El-Sayed also stands by his past comments on fighting discrimination aimed at those with HIV.

Last week, as he landed an endorsement from the Human Rights Campaign, a leading LGBTQ advocacy group, El-Sayed highlighted that if elected to the Senate, “I’ll fight to ensure every Michigander can live without discrimination and never have to wonder whether their rights will still be there tomorrow.”

El-Sayed, who narrowly edged more moderate Democratic Rep. Haley Stevens in August in a contentious primary that further exposed the rift between the party’s left-wing and establishment factions, would become the nation’s first Muslim senator if elected.

He has made support for “Medicare for all” a major component of his campaign.
